analysis.one_liner: Requires Supreme Court justices to follow a written code of conduct, disclose gifts, and step aside from conflicts.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the bill and put it on the Senate's calendar, but the Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would force the Supreme Court to adopt a code of conduct for justices, set up a process for filing and investigating misconduct complaints, and require justices to disclose gifts, income, and travel under standards at least as strict as those for members of Congress. It would expand the situations requiring a justice to step aside from a case, including when a party gave the justice gifts or spent money backing their appointment, and would make people filing Supreme Court briefs disclose their funders. The committee approved version also added a non-binding statement condemning racial attacks on Justice Clarence Thomas.
analysis.who_benefits: Litigants and the general public, who get a Supreme Court bound by written ethics rules, an actual complaint process, public disclosure of what gifts and money flow to justices, and clearer rules for when a justice must recuse. Ordinary people who appear before the federal courts would be litigating before judges whose financial ties to the parties are on the record.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Supreme Court to issue a code of conduct for justices and make it publicly available on the Court's website, and to establish procedures for individuals to file misconduct complaints, which a panel of five randomly chosen chief circuit judges would review and investigate.
Requires disclosure rules for justices' and law clerks' gifts, income, and reimbursements at least as rigorous as the disclosure rules that apply to the House and Senate.

Expands mandatory disqualification to cover cases where a party or its affiliate gave the justice, the justice's spouse, or minor children income, gifts, or reimbursements within a six-year window, or lobbied or spent substantial funds supporting the justice's appointment; justices must also notify parties when they learn of a possible conflict.

Requires parties and friends-of-the-court filers to disclose in their briefs any gift, income, or reimbursement they or their lawyers provided to a justice in the two years before a case, and requires amicus briefs to list major funders (over $100,000 or 3% of annual revenue), subject to an annual audit.
The Federal Judicial Center would study compliance with the recusal rules and report to Congress, and the Government Accountability Office would periodically evaluate the findings.

analysis.who_pays: The nine Supreme Court justices and the network around them: the justices themselves, wealthy patrons and major litigants whose gifts and financial ties would become public, and dark-money-funded groups that file anonymous friend-of-the-court briefs and would have to name their funders.

drawbacks.text: The expanded recusal rules sweep broadly: any gift or income from a party, its affiliates, or its lawyers within six years forces disqualification, and a denied recusal motion pauses the case until a panel rules, which parties could use strategically to remove justices from controversial cases or drag out proceedings.
A motion to disqualify a Supreme Court justice would be decided by the other eight justices, so in the highest-profile cases the Court would still be policing itself rather than an outside body.

The committee-added 'sense of Congress' section condemning racial attacks on Justice Thomas is a non-binding statement about public rhetoric that has nothing to do with the bill's ethics machinery, and critics of Congress mandating rules on the Court have long argued such requirements raise separation-of-powers objections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: the most powerful court in the country would go from no enforceable ethics code to written rules, a complaint process, and public disclosure of money and gifts. The main costs are design risks: the six-year gift lookback and motion-and-stay recusal procedure could be gamed to knock justices off cases, and letting the other eight justices review recusal motions keeps final judgment largely inside the Court. On balance the accountability gains outweigh the procedural risks, though the bill is not perfectly built.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee held a hearing, approved the bill with changes, and put it on the Senate's calendar of pending business, but no senator ever got a chance to vote on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on February 9, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
The Judiciary subcommittee on federal courts held a hearing on the bill on June 14, 2023.

On July 20, 2023, the Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment, and on September 5, 2023, Chairman Dick Durbin reported it to the Senate with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.
The committee-approved version added a Section 10, a non-binding 'sense of Congress' condemning racial attacks on Justice Clarence Thomas, alongside the ethics provisions.
On September 5, 2023, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 199, and no further action — no floor debate, no vote — ever occurred.

The bill drew 43 cosponsors, 42 of the 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 independents, and not a single Senate Republican, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still on the calendar.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The justices and the network of patrons, major litigants, and anonymous-funded brief-writers around the Court are better off: no enforceable code of conduct, no complaint process, no stricter gift disclosure, and no expanded recusal rules ever took effect. Meanwhile the Court's existing voluntary ethics code, adopted separately in November 2023, has no enforcement mechanism — though that development is outside the bill record here.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Supreme Court justices and their patrons

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Supreme Court ethics bill and recruited cosponsors across the Senate Democratic caucus.

for.name: Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Held a subcommittee hearing, managed the committee markup that reported the bill favorably, and reported it to the Senate with a substitute amendment.

for.name: 42 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the party leader, Schumer, and the committee's senior members.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 49 cosponsored the bill, and the Republican conference opposed the Court-ethics legislation; the bill never reached the floor for a vote.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, but as the senator who controls floor scheduling he never called it up for a vote while it sat on the Senate calendar for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 43 cosponsors was a Democrat or independent — 42 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 independents — with zero of 49 Senate Republicans signing on, and the bill died without a floor vote.

industries.note: The nine justices would go from having no enforceable ethics code to binding conduct rules, a public complaint process, gift and income disclosure as strict as members of Congress, and expanded recusal duties reaching gifts received up to six years earlier. Their interest in avoiding accountability ran directly against the public's interest in an impartial, transparent court.

industries.industry: Major litigants and wealthy patrons with ties to the Court
industries.note: Corporations, wealthy donors, and their lawyers with business before the Court would have to disclose any gifts, income, or reimbursements given to justices, and lobbying or spending that supported a justice's appointment would force the justice off their cases. Secrecy about these financial channels is what would be lost.

Groups filing friend-of-the-court briefs would have to name anyone who funded them above $100,000 or 3% of annual revenue, with an annual audit to check compliance. Anonymous-funded influence campaigns aimed at the Court would have to come out of the shadows.
